*4. (a) Suppose that f is continuous on [a,b] and that f(a) = f(b) = 0.
Suppose also that /(xo) > 0 for some xo in [n, Z?]. Prove that there are
numbers c and d with a<c<XQ<d<b such that /(c) = f(d) = 0,
but /(x) > 0 for all x in (c, d). Hint: The previous problem can be used
to good advantage.
(b) Suppose that / is continuous on [«, b] and that f(a) < f(b). Prove that
there are numbers c and d with a < c < d < b such that /(c) = f(a)
and /(d) = f(b) and /(a) < /(x) < f(d) for all x in (c,d).
5. (a) Suppose that y — x > 1. Prove that there is an integer k such that
x < k < y. Hint: Let I be the largest integer satisfying I < x, and
consider I + 1.
(b) Suppose x < y. Prove that there is a rational number r such that x <
r < y. Hint: If \/n < y — x, then ny — nx > 1. (Query: Why have parts
(a) and (b) been postponed until this problem set?)
(c) Suppose that r < s are rational numbers. Prove that there is an irrational
number between r and s. Hint: As a start, you know that there is an
irrational number between 0 and 1.
(d) Suppose that x < y. Prove that there is an irrational number between x 
and y. Hint: It is unnecessary to do any more work; this follows from
(b) and (c).
*6. A set A ofreal numbers is said to be dense if every open interval contains a
point of A. For example, Problem 5 shows that the set of rational numbers
and the set ofirrational numbers are each dense.
(a) Prove that if / is continuous and /(x) = 0 for all numbers x in a dense
set A, then /(x) = 0 for all x.
(b) Prove that if / and g are continuous and /(x) = g(x) for all x in a dense
set A, then /(x) = g(x) for all x.
(c) If we assume instead that /(x) > g(x) for all x in A, show that /(x) >
g(x) for all x. Can > be replaced by > throughout?
7. Prove that if / is continuous and /(x + y) = f(x) + /(y) for all x and y,
